What This Is

The Benson Increments Calculator estimates the standard enthalpy of formation of an organic molecule from Benson group increments. You choose the groups and corrections your molecule needs; it does the arithmetic and shows the working.

It is deliberately not a structure parser. The calculator does not inspect a molecule or decide which groups it requires, because deciding that is the skill being taught. The reasoning stays with you and the arithmetic stays visible.

Built for Chemistry C450/C540 at Indiana University Bloomington by Prashant Kumar and Nicola L. B. Pohl. The increment values follow Cohen and Benson (1993); the full citation, and everything else the numbers rest on, is in Sources and References at the foot of this page.

This page is the whole of the documentation. If something here is wrong or unclear, it is a file in reference/ and it can be fixed without touching any code — see the last section.

Using the Calculator

Click a group to add it, and click its count to take one back. The running total is always on screen, in kJ/mol and kcal/mol, headed by what it is a total of.

On a phone the total sits at the foot of the page — swipe it up, or press the button beside it, to see the working out.

Finding a group

You do not have to type Benson notation. Search by the shorthand you would write: CH3 finds C-(C)(H)3, and methylene finds C-(C)2(H)2. You can narrow to one category or several at once, which is normal — most molecules need groups from two or three of them.

Switch to the table view to see every value beside its unit, quantity and source.

Keyboard

  • Ctrl/Cmd + K — jump to the search box
  • arrow keys — move through the increments
  • Enter — add the one in focus
  • + / - — adjust its count

Getting the working out

Copy puts the whole calculation on the clipboard as plain text, laid out as a column so it lines up when pasted into a report. Undo takes back the last addition and Reset clears everything.

The Method

Benson group additivity estimates the standard enthalpy of formation of a molecule by adding up contributions from its parts. You identify the groups the molecule is made of, look up what each one contributes, and sum them. That sum is the estimate. There is no other step.

A group is one polyvalent atom together with the ligands bonded to it. The central atom is what the group is of; the ligands describe the neighbourhood it sits in. So a carbon bonded to one carbon and three hydrogens is written C-(C)(H)3, and it is worth −42 kJ/mol wherever it appears — in propane, in toluene, in a steroid.

Why a group and not an atom or a bond? Because there is a ladder of approximations, and the group is the rung that works. Adding up atoms is the zeroth-order approximation and is poor. Adding up bonds is first-order and is better, but a C–H bond in a methyl group is not identical to a C–H bond next to a carbonyl, and the difference is large enough to matter. Adding up groups is the second-order approximation: because a group carries the central atom's whole neighbourhood, the environment that makes those two C–H bonds differ is already written into it.

What it does not capture is anything that depends on the shape of the whole molecule: ring strain, two substituents crowding each other, a cis double bond forcing groups together. Those are handled by corrections, which are added once per ring or per interaction rather than once per atom.

The calculator deliberately does not inspect a structure or decide which groups a molecule needs. You choose them. The method is the thing being taught, so the reasoning stays in your hands and the arithmetic stays visible.

Reading a Group Name

Every group name has the same shape: the central atom, a dash, then the ligands in brackets with a count where there is more than one.

C-(C)2(H)2 is a carbon bonded to two carbons and two hydrogens — the methylene of an alkane chain. CO-(C)2 is a carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbons, which is to say a ketone.

The ligands are not counted twice

A ligand says what the central atom is bonded to. It does not contribute that atom to the molecule. In C-(C)3(H), the three bracketed carbons are each counted by their own group; counting them here as well would give every carbon one extra for each neighbour it happens to have.

Hydrogen is the exception, and today the only one. A hydrogen never has a group of its own, so the group it is written in is the only place it is ever counted.

Searching by what you would write

You do not have to type Benson notation to find a group. The calculator reads the notation, so a carbon with three hydrogen ligands is findable as CH3 even though those three characters appear nowhere in C-(C)(H)3. Common names work too — methyl, ketone, hydroxyl — and are listed in notation/synonyms.csv.

Notation

NotationWhat it isChecked against
CA saturated carbon: four single bonds.Benson 1976
CdA carbon of a C=C double bond ("d" for double), as in an alkene.Benson 1976
CtA carbon of a C≡C triple bond ("t" for triple), as in an alkyne.Benson 1976
CBAn aromatic carbon in a benzene ring ("B" for benzene).Benson 1976
COA carbonyl carbon taken together with its oxygen, C=O.not yet
OA divalent oxygen: the oxygen of an ether, an alcohol or an ester.not yet
NAn amine nitrogen: three single bonds.Ashcraft & Green 2008
CNThe carbon of a nitrile, C≡N, taken together with its nitrogen.Ashcraft & Green 2008
NO2The nitrogen of a nitro group, taken with its two oxygens.Ashcraft & Green 2008
ONOA nitrite ester, R–O–N=O.Ashcraft & Green 2008
NIA doubly-bonded imino nitrogen, as in an imine or an oxime. Contributes its nitrogen only; the carbon of the C=N is counted by its own CdN group.Ashcraft & Green 2008
CdNThe carbon of a C=N double bond — a Cd whose partner is nitrogen. Contributes its carbon only. See the note below.not yet
NCAn isocyanide, R–N≡C. The one value here is NC-(C), and C-(H)3(N) + NC-(C) = −42 + 210 = 168 kJ/mol against a measured 163.5 ± 7.2 for methyl isocyanide.NIST WebBook
[COd]The four ketene rows. How many heavy atoms they stand for is an open question, recorded in notation/README.md.not yet

What Is Not Yet Confirmed

The last column of the Notation table records what each description was checked against. It is about the prose, not the arithmetic: every value in the calculator is the published one and is used exactly as it stands, and what is being checked is the sentence describing the bonding beside it.

Four entries still read not yet. CO and O are ordinary and almost certainly right; they are simply unchecked. [COd] is a genuine open question, already recorded in notation/README.md. CdN is the interesting one.

The nitrogen in a C=N is counted twice

notation/central_atoms.csv records CdN as contributing a carbon and a nitrogen, while NI contributes a nitrogen. Both appear in the same molecule, so the nitrogen is counted twice. Methanimine, CH2=NH, has one nitrogen, and the two groups it is made of give two:

CdN-(H)2 + NI-(H) -> C1 N2 H3

The thermochemistry points the same way. Read with CdN contributing only its carbon, methanimine is 28 + 64 = 92 kJ/mol, against measurements spanning 69 ± 8 to 110 ± 8 kJ/mol. Read with CdN carrying the nitrogen as well — so that no NI group is added — it is 28 kJ/mol, far below every measured value.

So CdN should almost certainly contribute C alone, exactly as Cd does. That is one cell in notation/central_atoms.csv.

Nothing in the calculator is affected today. The atom counting feeds a molecular-formula check that is deliberately switched off, and every enthalpy comes straight from the CSV files, untouched by any of this. It is written down here so that whoever switches that check on meets it first.

Glossary

TermWhat it means
Group incrementThe contribution one group makes to the standard enthalpy of formation. It is the number on each button in the calculator, in kJ/mol.
CorrectionA term added once per ring or per interaction rather than once per atom. Corrections carry what group additivity cannot see on its own: ring strain, a gauche interaction, two substituents crowding each other across a double bond.
A-valueThe free-energy cost of a substituent sitting axial rather than equatorial on a cyclohexane ring. A larger A-value means a stronger preference for the equatorial position — a tert-butyl group, at about 20 kJ/mol, is almost never axial.
ΔHf°Standard enthalpy of formation: the enthalpy change on forming one mole of a substance from its elements in their standard states. This is what the group increments and corrections sum to.
ΔG°Standard Gibbs free energy change. The cyclohexane A-values are free energies, not enthalpies, which is why the calculator will not head a total ΔHf° once one of them is in the sum.
LigandAn atom or group written in brackets in a group name, describing what the central atom is bonded to. A ligand is not counted as an atom of the molecule; hydrogen is the exception.
Central atomThe polyvalent atom a group is built around — the part of the name before the dash.
Averaged rangeA value the source published as a span rather than a single number, such as 2.51-4.35. The calculator sums the midpoint and shows the span beside it.
kJ/molKilojoules per mole, the unit every value in this calculator is stored in.
kcal/molKilocalories per mole. Shown alongside kJ/mol for comparison with older literature; 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.

Why a Range Is Averaged

Fifteen of the twenty-nine cyclohexane A-values are published as a range rather than a single number — the hydroxyl A-value is given as 2.51-4.35 kJ/mol. The range is real: it reflects genuine disagreement between the solvents and methods the measurements came from, not sloppiness.

A sum needs one number, so the calculator uses the midpoint. That is a fair thing to add up and a misleading thing to print on its own, because 3.43 looks like a measurement and is not one. So the published range is shown beside the value everywhere the value appears, and the running total reports how far it could move if every averaged range in the sum were read at its bounds instead of its middle.

Precision is handled the same way. A value is shown to the number of decimal places its source actually claims: 195 of the 236 increments are written as plain integers, so the calculator prints −42 rather than −42.00, which would assert two decimals Cohen & Benson never published. An averaged range is the one exception, since the midpoint of two two-decimal bounds can need a third place — 1.05-1.76 averages to 1.405.

Worked Examples

Three molecules, worked the way you would work them in the calculator. Every increment below is the one in this repository's CSV files, so you can check each line against the buttons on the calculator page. The measured values are from the NIST Chemistry WebBook, for gas-phase ΔHf° at 298 K.

Butane

Four carbons: two methyls at the ends, two methylenes in the middle.

  • C-(C)(H)3 × 2 = −84.0
  • C-(C)2(H)2 × 2 = −41.8
  • Estimate −125.8 kJ/mol — measured −125.6 ± 0.67 (Pittam and Pilcher, 1972)

Ethanol

The point of this one is that its groups come from two different files — the CH groups and the CHO groups. Crossing two or three categories is normal, and the calculator lets you filter several at once for exactly this reason.

  • C-(C)(H)3 = −42
  • C-(H)2(O)(C) = −33
  • O-(H)(C) = −159
  • Estimate −234.0 kJ/mol — measured −234 ± 2 (average of nine values)

Cyclohexane

Six identical methylenes — and then a correction, because six methylenes in a ring are not the same as six in a chain. This is what corrections are for.

  • C-(C)2(H)2 × 6 = −125.4
  • cyclohexane correction = +2
  • Estimate −123.4 kJ/mol — measured −123.1 ± 0.79 (Prosen, Johnson et al.,

1946)

Without the correction the estimate would be −125.4, and the ring would be indistinguishable from six carbons of a chain. The correction is added once for the ring, not once per carbon in it.

A word about how well these agree

All three land within about half a kJ/mol of experiment, which is better than the method's own typical accuracy and better than you should expect in general. These are easy molecules: unstrained, monofunctional, and among the compounds whose measured values went into deriving the increments in the first place. Reported accuracies for group additivity run from roughly 2 to 10 kJ/mol depending on the compound and whose group values are used, and multifunctional or strained molecules are where it does worst. An estimate is an estimate.

What not to add together

A cyclohexane A-value is a free energy, not an enthalpy of formation. Adding the methyl A-value of 7.28 to the ΔHf° above does not give you the enthalpy of anything. The calculator will let you select both — sometimes you want both on screen — but it stops heading the total ΔHf° the moment the sum stops being one, and says plainly what it has been mixed with.

The Five Categories

The calculator holds 236 values in five categories. They are not all the same physical quantity, which is why the running total is careful about what it calls itself.

The table below is not written out here — it is read directly from notation/categories.csv, the file the calculator itself uses to decide how to head a total. There is one description of a category in this repository, not two that can disagree.

FileQuantitySymbolUnitSourceNote
01_CH_Groups.csvstandard enthalpy of formationΔHf°kJ/molCohen & Benson 1993
02_CHO_Groups.csvstandard enthalpy of formationΔHf°kJ/molCohen & Benson 1993
03_CHNO_Groups.csvstandard enthalpy of formationΔHf°kJ/molCohen & Benson 1993
04_Corrections.csvring and steric correctionΔHf°kJ/molCohen & Benson 1993Added once per ring or interaction rather than per atom
05_Cyclohexane_A_Values.csvconformational free-energy preferenceΔG°kJ/molAxial substituent penalty. Not an enthalpy of formation. 15 of the 29 values are published as ranges

The Source cell for the A-values is empty on purpose. Where those values came from cannot be established from anything in this repository, and an invented citation would be worse than an admitted gap. If you can identify the source, that empty cell is the place to put it.
